17592186092083.question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^3 - x^2$ at the point $(1,0)$ is given by $y=px+q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the values of $p$ and $q.$
17592186092083.question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=x^3 - x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-{x}^{2})=3{x}^{2}-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1, 0){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=3-2=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line $m'$ is

$$
m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =-(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-1$ and $q=1.$

$$

     

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1) = (1)^{-1/2} - 4 = -3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{3}x & =\frac{7}{3} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}

Find where the normal line to the curve $y=2\sqrt{x}+3x$ at the point with $x$-coordinate $1$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The intersection is $(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$. Give exact values.

First find the point on the curve.

$$
f(1)=2\sqrt{(1)}+3(1)=5.
$$

The normal passes through $(1,5)$.

Rewrite the radical or reciprocal using powers, then differentiate.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=2 x^{\frac{1}{2}} + 3 x, \\f'(x)&=3 + \frac{1}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}=3 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the tangent slope and take its negative reciprocal to find the normal slope.

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_t=f'(1)&=3 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1)}}=4, \\m_n=-\frac{1}{m_t}&=-\frac{1}{(4)}=- \frac{1}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use point-slope form through $(1,5)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-(5)&=- \frac{1}{4}(x-(1)), \\y&=- \frac{x}{4} + \frac{21}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $x$-axis, $y=0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
0&=- \frac{1}{4}x+\left(\frac{21}{4}\right), \\x&=21.
\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection is $(21,0)$.
